{{Short description|English physicist}}
'''Alexander Michael Hillas''' (June 1932 – 26 November 2017)<ref name=timeshighereducation>{{cite web|url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/people/obituary-michael-hillas-1932-2017 |title=Michael Hillas, 1932-2017 |date=21 December 2017 }}</ref> was an English [[cosmic ray]] physicist. He is known for the [[Gaisser–Hillas function]],<ref>{{cite conference
  | last = Gaisser
  | first = T.K.
  | author2 = Hillas, A.M.
  | title = Reliability of the method of constant intensity cuts for reconstructing the average development of vertical showers
  | journal = 
  | book-title = Proc. of 15th Int. Cosmic Ray Conf., 13–26 Aug 1977
  | place = Plovdiv, Bulgaria
  | date = 1977
  | volume = 8
  | pages = 353
  | bibcode = 1977ICRC....8..353G
  }}</ref> the Hillas parameters,<ref>{{cite journal|author=de Naurois, Mathieu|author2=Rolland, Loïc|year=2009|title=A high performance likelihood reconstruction of γ-rays for imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes|journal=Astroparticle Physics |volume=32 |issue=5 |pages=231–252 |doi=10.1016/j.astropartphys.2009.09.001 |arxiv=0907.2610|bibcode=2009APh....32..231D }}</ref> and MOCCA, a [[Monte Carlo]] [[Source code|computer code]] used for simulation of extensive [[Air shower (physics)|air shower]]s (EASs) in the energy range from 10<sup>12</sup> (tera-) [[Electronvolt|eV]] to 10<sup>21</sup> (zetta-) eV.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/S0920-5632(96)00847-X |title=Shower simulation: Lessons from MOCCA |date=1997 |last1=Hillas |first1=A.M. |journal=Nuclear Physics B - Proceedings Supplements |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=29–42 |bibcode=1997NuPhS..52...29H }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Reininghaus, M.|author2=Ulrich, R.|author3=Pierog, T.|year=2021|title= Proceedings of 37th International Cosmic Ray Conference — PoS(ICRC2021)|chapter=Air shower genealogy for muon production |page=463 |doi=10.22323/1.395.0463 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2108.03266}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born in a village near [[Leeds]], A. Michael Hillas attended school in [[York]].<ref name=timeshighereducation/> He studied at [[Bootham School]] from 1947 to 1950.<ref>{{cite web|title=obituaries - Bootham Old Scholars Online Community|website=oldscholars.boothamschool.com|url=https://oldscholars.boothamschool.com/ocd.aspx?action=check_bulletin&bulletin_name=obituaries&code=&menuItem=Obituaries}}</ref> In secondary school, he showed remarkable signs of talent for computation.<ref name=Watson>{{cite web|author=Watson, Alan|date=December 10, 2018|title=Michael Hillas, Hillas Symposium at Heidelberg|url=https://www.mpi-hd.mpg.de/hillas2018/slides/Hillas2018_01_Watson.pdf}}</ref> At the [[University of Leeds]], he graduated with a B.Sc. in physics in 1955<ref name=Auger>{{cite web|title=Obituary of Michael Hillas|website=Pierre Auger Observatory (auger.org)|url=https://www.auger.org/images/PDFs/2017-11_Obituary_Michael-Hillas.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite conference  | last = Gaisser  | first = T.K.  | author2 = Hillas, A.M.  | title = Reliability of the method of constant intensity cuts for reconstructing the average development of vertical showers  | journal =   | book-title = Proc. of 15th Int. Cosmic Ray Conf., 13–26 Aug 1977  | place = Plovdiv, Bulgaria  | date = 1977  | volume = 8  | pages = 353  | bibcode = 1977ICRC....8..353G  }}</ref> with First Class Honours<ref name=Watson/> and with a Ph.D. in 1958.<ref name=Auger/> His Ph.D. thesis is entitled ''The interaction of stopped negative muons with atomic nuclei''.<ref name=Watson/> As a postdoc, Hillas held a fellowship at [[Harwell Science and Innovation Campus]].<ref name=Auger/> In 1959 at Harwell, Michael Hillas and Thomas Edwin "Ted" Cranshaw (1922–2016) measured, with extreme accuracy, the charge difference between the [[proton]] and the [[electron]].<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1038/184892a0 |title=A Comparison of the Charges of the Electron, Proton and Neutron |date=1959 |last1=Hillas |first1=A. M. |last2=Cranshaw |first2=T. E. |journal=Nature |volume=184 |issue=4690 |pages=892–893 |bibcode=1959Natur.184..892H }}</ref> (Cranshaw was nominated for a Nobel Prize in 1966 by Yukihisa "Yuki" Nogami,<ref>{{cite web|title=T. E. Crenshaw, Nomination Archive|website=nobelprize.org|date=21 May 2024 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/show_people.php?id=14254}}</ref> a former doctoral student of [[Hideki Yukawa]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://physics.mcmaster.ca/people/faculty/Nogami_Y_h.html|title=Yukihisa Nogami, Professor Emeritus|website=McMaster University}}</ref>) Hillas worked at Harwell on an experiment to study air showers from cosmic rays. The experiment used an array of approximately 90 [[Geiger counter]]s deployed over an area of .6 km<sup>2</sup> (about 148 acres).<ref name=Auger/> As part of the experimental team, he had to get up at night to repair cables that had been bitten through by rabbits. The Harwell Safety Officer William Galbraith was alarmed by the way Hillas waded around wet enclosures that housed Geiger counters for muons and had [[kilovolt]]s of dangerous [[voltage]].<ref name=Watson/>

== Career ==
Hillas returned to the [[University of Leeds]] in 1959 as a lecturer.<ref name=Auger/> Professor John Graham Wilson (1911–1994) at the University of Leeds initiated the study of cosmic rays in a project implemented at [[Haverah Park]]<ref>{{cite web|title=History of High Energy Astrophysics at Leeds|website=Astrophysics Group, University of Leeds|url=https://ast.leeds.ac.uk/about/history-of-high-energy-astrophysics-at-leeds/}}</ref> and persuaded Hillas to work on the interpretation of data from the project. At the University of Leeds, Hillas was promoted in 1969 from lectureship to readership and in 1990 to a professorial chair in physics. In retirement, he remained in the department of physics and astronomy as a research professor working on TeV ([[Electronvolt|tera-electronvolt]]) [[gamma-ray]] astronomy. He did outstanding research in numerical modelling for cosmic ray physics. His Monte Carlo computer program, MOCCA, for high-energy air shower studies, was used extensively in the design of the [[Pierre Auger Observatory]]. MOCCA was written in [[Pascal (programming language)|Pascal]] and was widely used by the Auger Collaboration (despite their unfamiliarity of the computer language Pascal) and, notably, by the Nobel Laureate, [[James Cronin]], during a sabbatical visit to the University Leeds in 1991. MOCCA was eventually translated into [[FORTRAN]].<ref name=Auger/>

Hillas combined outstanding talents as a numerical modeller with good physical insight, as well as considerable ability as an experimentalist.<ref name=Auger/> He gained an international reputation as a pioneer of selecting gamma-ray images based on their predicted properties.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1989ApJ...342..379W/abstract |bibcode=1989ApJ...342..379W |title=Observation of TeV Gamma Rays from the Crab Nebula Using the Atmospheric Cerenkov Imaging Technique |last1=Weekes |first1=T. C. |last2=Cawley |first2=M. F. |last3=Fegan |first3=D. J. |last4=Gibbs |first4=K. G. |last5=Hillas |first5=A. M. |last6=Kowk |first6=P. W. |last7=Lamb |first7=R. C. |last8=Lewis |first8=D. A. |last9=MacOmb |first9=D. |last10=Porter |first10=N. A. |last11=Reynolds |first11=P. T. |last12=Vacanti |first12=G. |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |date=1989 |volume=342 |page=379 |doi=10.1086/167599 }}</ref> In the late 1980s, Hillas published his ideas about techniques for distinguishing between gamma rays and hadrons in the cosmic rays at energies around one tera-electronvolt (1 TeV). The concept involves using large mirrors to detect the [[Cherenkov radiation]] which these low-energy cosmic-rays produce in Earth's atmosphere. The "Hillas parameters" are used world-wide in cosmic ray research and play an essential role for the [[Cherenkov Telescope Array]], which detects gamma rays in the energy range from 10 [[GeV]] to about 300 TeV.<ref name=Auger/> In the early part of the 21st century he was a member of the [[VERITAS]] science team.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.newar.2003.12.050 |title=VERITAS: The Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System |date=2004 |last1=Krennrich |first1=F. |last2=Bond |first2=I.H. |last3=Boyle |first3=P.J. |last4=Bradbury |first4=S.M. |last5=Buckley |first5=J.H. |last6=Carter-Lewis |first6=D. |last7=Celik |first7=O. |last8=Cui |first8=W. |last9=Daniel |first9=M. |last10=d'Vali |first10=M. |last11=de la Calle Perez |first11=I. |last12=Duke |first12=C. |last13=Falcone |first13=A. |last14=Fegan |first14=D.J. |last15=Fegan |first15=S.J. |last16=Finley |first16=J.P. |last17=Fortson |first17=L.F. |last18=Gaidos |first18=J. |last19=Gammell |first19=S. |last20=Gibbs |first20=K. |last21=Gillanders |first21=G.H. |last22=Grube |first22=J. |last23=Hall |first23=J. |last24=Hall |first24=T.A. |last25=Hanna |first25=D. |last26=Hillas |first26=A.M. |last27=Holder |first27=J. |last28=Horan |first28=D. |last29=Jarvis |first29=A. |last30=Jordan |first30=M. |journal=New Astronomy Reviews |volume=48 |issue=5–6 |pages=345–349 |display-authors=1 |bibcode=2004NewAR..48..345K |hdl=10379/9414 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
In 1998 the [[Institute of Physics]] (IOP) awarded Hillas the institute's Rutherford Medal and Prize.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ernest Rutherford Medal and Prize recipients|website=Institute of Physics (IOP)|
url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/silver-subject-medals/ernest-rutherford-medal-and-prize-recipients}}</ref> In 2005 the Commission on Astrophysical Particles of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]] (IUPAP) awarded him the [[Yodh Prize]] “for his significant and outstanding contributions to the field of cosmic ray astrophysics”.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ps.uci.edu/~yodhprize/recipients.html |title=Yodh Prize: Past Recipients |website=School of Physical Sciences, UC Irvine}} (award sponsored by University of California Irvine Foundation & administered by [[IUPAP]])</ref>
